s: Exodus 1 lists the sons of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob, seventy souls in all, with Joseph already there. After Joseph and his generation died, the Israelites multiplied greatly and filled the land. A new king of Egypt who did not know Joseph feared their numbers and set taskmasters over them, forcing them into hard labor building the storage cities Pithom and Raamses. When they kept multiplying, the king ordered the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill newborn boys, but the midwives feared God and let them live, and God gave them families. Pharaoh then commanded all his people to cast every newborn son into the river while saving the daughters alive.

l: children of Israel, Exodus, Exodus / Chapter 1
s: The sons of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob are named, totaling seventy souls. After Joseph and his generation died, they grew exceedingly numerous and mighty, and the land was filled with them. Despite affliction they kept multiplying and spreading out, and the Egyptians came to dread them.

Egypt is where Joseph already was and where the sons of Israel came with Jacob's household. Its land was filled with the multiplying Israelites, and its new king viewed them as a threat. Israelites built the storage cities Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh there.

A new king arose who did not know Joseph and feared that the more numerous Israelites might join Egypt's enemies in war and leave the land. He set taskmasters over them, then ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys. When the midwives defied him and gave an excuse, he commanded all his people to cast every newborn son into the river and keep the daughters alive.

The Egyptians began to dread the children of Israel as they multiplied despite affliction. They ruthlessly made the Israelites serve, making their lives bitter with hard labor in mortar, brick, and field work. Pharaoh commanded all his people to throw every Hebrew son into the river.

Shiphrah and Puah were told by the king of Egypt to kill Hebrew baby boys at birth but feared God and saved the boys alive. When questioned, they told Pharaoh that Hebrew women are vigorous and give birth before the midwife arrives. God dealt well with them and gave them families.
God is the one the midwives feared, which led them to disobey the king's command. He dealt well with the midwives, giving them families, and the people multiplied and grew very mighty.

l: Hebrew baby boys (sons born to Hebrew women), Exodus, Exodus / Chapter 1
s: The king of Egypt ordered the midwives to kill the boys at birth while letting the daughters live, but the midwives saved the boys alive. Pharaoh then commanded that every son born be cast into the river.

l: forced labor of Israelites, Exodus, Exodus / Chapter 1
s: Taskmasters were set over the Israelites to afflict them with burdens, and they built the storage cities Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh. The Egyptians ruthlessly made them serve in mortar, brick, and all kinds of field work, making their lives bitter. The oppression did not stop their growth, as they multiplied and spread out all the more.

A Levite woman hides her newborn son for three months, then places him in a tar-coated papyrus basket among the reeds by the river, while his sister watches. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, takes pity, and through the sister hires the child's own mother as nurse; he becomes the princess's son and she names him Moses. As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian who was striking a Hebrew, and when a Hebrew challenges him the next day, he realizes the deed is known; Pharaoh seeks to kill him and he flees to Midian. There he helps the priest Reuel's seven daughters at a well, is welcomed by Reuel, marries Zipporah, and has a son named Gershom. Meanwhile the king of Egypt dies, the Israelites cry out under bondage, and God hears, remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and sees them.

Moses is born to a Levite couple, hidden for three months, set in a basket by the river, and drawn out by Pharaoh's daughter, who adopts him and names him. Grown, he kills an Egyptian who was striking a Hebrew and hides the body, then flees to Midian when Pharaoh seeks to kill him. In Midian he helps Reuel's daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and has a son named Gershom, saying he has lived as a foreigner in a foreign land.

l: Moses' mother (woman of the house of Levi), Exodus, Chapter 2
s: She is a daughter of Levi who bears a fine son and hides him three months. When she can no longer hide him, she places him in a tar-coated papyrus basket in the reeds. She is later called by her daughter and hired by Pharaoh's daughter to nurse her own child for wages.
She stands far off to watch what will happen to the baby in the basket. When Pharaoh's daughter finds him, she offers to fetch a Hebrew nurse and, told to go, brings the child's mother.

She comes to bathe at the river, finds the basket, and has compassion on the crying baby, recognizing him as a Hebrew child. She hires his mother as nurse, adopts the boy as her son, and names him Moses because she drew him out of the water.

The baby is identified as one of the Hebrews' children, and Hebrew women are the source of a possible nurse. Moses sees their burdens and sees an Egyptian strike a Hebrew. The next day two Hebrews fight each other, and the one in the wrong challenges Moses' authority and reveals knowledge of the killing.
He is seen striking a Hebrew, one of Moses' brothers. Moses kills him when no one is watching and hides his body in the sand.

Reuel is the priest of Midian and father of seven daughters. When they return early from watering the flock and tell him an Egyptian helped them, he orders them to call the man to eat bread. He then gives his daughter Zipporah to Moses, who is content to dwell with him.
Zipporah is a daughter of Reuel, given to Moses as his wife. She bears a son, whom Moses names Gershom.

After the king of Egypt dies, the children of Israel sigh and cry out because of their bondage, and their cry rises to God. God hears their groaning, sees them, and remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

God hears the Israelites' groaning, remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, sees the children of Israel, and understands. No action is yet taken in this unit beyond his attention to their plight.

l: forced labor of Israelites, Exodus, Chapter 2
s: The Israelites groan under bondage that continues past the death of the king of Egypt. Their cry because of it comes up to God, who hears it.

l: Moses' killing of the Egyptian, Exodus, Chapter 2
s: Moses looks around, sees no one, kills an Egyptian who was striking a Hebrew, and hides him in the sand. The next day a Hebrew he rebukes refers to it, and Moses realizes it is known. Pharaoh hears of it and seeks to kill Moses, who flees to Midian.

While keeping the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, Moses comes to Horeb, God's mountain, and sees a bush that burns without being consumed. God calls to him from the bush, identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and says he has seen the affliction of his people in Egypt. God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring the children of Israel out toward a land flowing with milk and honey. Moses objects and asks what name to give the people, and God answers 'I AM WHO I AM' and calls himself the LORD, the God of their fathers. God instructs Moses to gather the elders, predicts that the king of Egypt will refuse until God strikes Egypt with wonders, and promises that the Israelites will plunder the Egyptians when they leave.

Moses keeps Jethro's flock, goes to Horeb, and turns aside to see the burning bush. He hides his face when God speaks, then asks 'Who am I?' and what name to tell the Israelites. He is sent to Pharaoh and to the elders of Israel to bring the people out of Egypt.

God calls to Moses from the bush, declares himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and says he has seen the Israelites' affliction and come down to deliver them. He commissions Moses, promises to be with him, and foretells that Pharaoh will refuse until he strikes Egypt with wonders. He also promises the people will leave with favor and plunder.

Horeb is called God's mountain, where Moses arrives while leading the flock to the back of the wilderness. It is made holy ground by God's presence. God says that after the people leave Egypt they will serve him on this mountain, as a token to Moses.
The bush burns with fire in which the LORD's angel appears, yet it is not consumed. It draws Moses to look, and God calls to him from the middle of it.

The Israelites, called God's people and the children of Israel, are afflicted by taskmasters in Egypt, and their cry has reached God. God promises to bring them out to a good and large land. Their elders will listen to Moses, and the people will ask for silver, gold, and clothing from the Egyptians.
Egypt is the land where God's people are afflicted and from which God will bring them up. God says he will strike it with all his wonders, after which its king will let the people go.

The Egyptians oppress the Israelites through taskmasters, and God says he will deliver the people from their hand. God will give the Israelites favor in their sight, so the women ask for jewels of silver, jewels of gold, and clothing, and so plunder them.

Pharaoh, called the king of Egypt, is the one Moses is sent to. God says he will not give permission to go, not even by a mighty hand, and will let the people go only after God strikes Egypt with wonders.

God promises to bring the Israelites to a good and large land flowing with milk and honey. It is described as the place of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.

When Moses asks what name to give, God says 'I AM WHO I AM' and tells him to say 'I AM has sent me to you.' God also says he is the LORD, the God of the fathers, and that this is his name forever and his memorial to all generations.

Moses fears the Israelites will not believe him, so the LORD gives him signs: his rod turns into a snake and back, his hand becomes leprous and is restored, and river water will turn to blood. When Moses protests that he is slow of speech and asks the LORD to send someone else, the LORD becomes angry and appoints his brother Aaron as spokesman. Moses gets permission from Jethro, his father-in-law, to return to Egypt with his wife and sons, carrying God's rod, and the LORD tells him he will harden Pharaoh's heart and that Pharaoh's firstborn will be killed if he refuses. On the way the LORD meets Moses and wants to kill him until his wife Zipporah circumcises her son. Aaron meets Moses at God's mountain, and together they gather the elders, perform the signs, and the people believe and worship.

Moses doubts that the people will believe him and objects that he is slow of speech, asking the LORD to send someone else. After the LORD's anger and the appointment of Aaron, he gets Jethro's blessing, takes his wife and sons and God's rod, and returns toward Egypt. The LORD meets him at a lodging place and wants to kill him, but relents after Zipporah circumcises their son; Moses then tells Aaron all the LORD's words and gathers the elders.

The LORD gives Moses signs with the rod, the hand, and river water, and answers his protest by asserting that he made man's mouth and will teach Moses what to say. He grows angry at Moses' request for someone else, appoints Aaron as spokesman, and tells Moses he will harden Pharaoh's heart and kill Pharaoh's firstborn, calling Israel his firstborn son. He meets Moses at a lodging place and wants to kill him, but lets him alone after the circumcision, and the people believe that he has visited them.

Aaron, Moses' brother the Levite, is described by the LORD as a good speaker who is coming out to meet Moses and will be glad to see him. He is to be Moses' mouth to the people. He meets Moses on God's mountain and kisses him, speaks all the LORD's words to the elders, and performs the signs before the people.

The Israelites are called the LORD's son, his firstborn, whom Pharaoh is to let go to serve him. Moses worries they will not believe him, but when Aaron speaks and does the signs, they believe. On hearing that the LORD had visited them and seen their affliction, they bow their heads and worship.

Pharaoh is the one Moses is to confront with the wonders, though the LORD says he will harden Pharaoh's heart so that he will not let the people go. Moses is to tell him that the LORD says to let his son Israel go, and that his own firstborn son will be killed if he refuses.

Egypt is where Moses' brothers, the Israelites, remain, and where he asks Jethro to let him return to see if they are alive. The LORD tells him to go back because the men who sought his life are dead, and Moses travels there with his wife and sons.

The rod in Moses' hand becomes a snake when thrown down and a rod again when he takes it by the tail, as a sign that the LORD has appeared to him. The LORD tells him to take it to do the signs, and Moses takes it as God's rod on his journey to Egypt.

The LORD gives Moses three signs so that the people will believe: the rod turning into a snake, the hand turning leprous and then restored, and river water becoming blood on dry land. Moses tells Aaron about them, and Aaron performs them before the people, who believe.

Moses and Aaron come to Pharaoh with the LORD's demand to let Israel go to hold a feast in the wilderness, but Pharaoh refuses, saying he does not know the LORD. He accuses the people of idleness and orders his taskmasters and officers to stop supplying straw while demanding the same number of bricks. The people scatter across Egypt to gather stubble, and the Israelite officers are beaten when the quota is not met. The officers appeal to Pharaoh, who rejects them and repeats that the people are idle. The officers then blame Moses and Aaron for making them a stench to Pharaoh, and Moses asks the LORD why he has brought trouble on the people and has not rescued them.

Moses, with Aaron, delivers the LORD's message to Pharaoh asking that Israel be let go to hold a feast, and is refused. The officers of Israel accuse him of making them a stench in Pharaoh's eyes. Moses returns to the LORD and complains that the LORD has brought trouble on the people and has not rescued them at all.
Aaron accompanies Moses to Pharaoh and speaks the LORD's demand. He stands with Moses on the road when the Israelite officers come out from Pharaoh and blame them both.

Pharaoh says he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go, and he tells Moses and Aaron to get back to their burdens. He commands that straw no longer be given while the brick count stays the same, calls the people idle, and rejects the officers' appeal.

The LORD, the God of Israel, is named by Moses and Aaron as the one who demands that his people be let go to hold a feast in the wilderness. Pharaoh denies knowing him. At the end Moses questions him, saying that he has brought trouble on the people and has not rescued them.

The Israelites are told to gather their own straw and are scattered throughout Egypt to find stubble, while still required to produce the same number of bricks. Their workload becomes heavier, and their officers are beaten when the quota falls short.

Pharaoh's taskmasters receive his command and tell the people that no straw will be given. They press the people urgently to fulfill the daily quota as when there was straw, and they beat the Israelite officers when it is not met.

l: officers of the children of Israel, Exodus, Chapter 5
s: The Israelite officers, set over the people by Pharaoh's taskmasters, are beaten and questioned about the missed quota. They cry out to Pharaoh, are rebuffed, and then tell Moses and Aaron that the LORD should look at them and judge, because they have made the officers a stench to Pharaoh and his servants.

Pharaoh orders that straw no longer be supplied for making brick and that the people gather it themselves. The people are scattered across Egypt to gather stubble for straw, and the officers complain that none is given to them.

l: bricks (the daily brick quota), Exodus, Chapter 5
s: Pharaoh insists the number of bricks not be diminished even without straw provided. Failure to meet the daily quota leads to beatings of the Israelite officers, and Pharaoh repeats the demand to deliver the same number.

l: feast and sacrifice to the LORD, Exodus, Chapter 5
s: Moses and Aaron ask that the people be allowed a three-day journey into the wilderness to hold a feast and sacrifice to the LORD, lest he fall on them with pestilence or the sword. Pharaoh rejects the request and treats the people's desire to sacrifice as evidence of idleness.

The LORD tells Moses he will see what is done to Pharaoh, and identifies himself as the God who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty but was not known to them by the name the LORD. He declares he has heard Israel's groaning, remembered his covenant, and promises to redeem the children of Israel from Egyptian bondage and bring them to the land sworn to the patriarchs. Moses relays this, but the people do not listen because of anguish and cruel bondage. When the LORD commands Moses to speak to Pharaoh, Moses objects that he has uncircumcised lips. A genealogy of the heads of fathers' houses of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi follows, tracing Aaron and Moses through Amram and Jochebed, and the chapter closes with the LORD repeating the command and Moses repeating his objection.

The LORD announces that Pharaoh will let Israel go by a strong hand, and says he appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty but was not known to them by his name the LORD. He promises to bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as his people, and give them the land he swore to the patriarchs. He commands Moses to speak to Pharaoh, and gives Moses and Aaron a command concerning Israel and Pharaoh.

Moses relays the LORD's promises to the children of Israel, but they do not listen. When told to speak to Pharaoh, he objects twice that Israel has not listened to him and that he has uncircumcised lips. The genealogy identifies him as a son of Amram and Jochebed, and as one of the Moses and Aaron the LORD told to bring Israel out of Egypt.

Aaron is addressed with Moses in the LORD's command to bring Israel out of Egypt. The genealogy names him as a son of Amram and Jochebed, husband of Elisheba, and father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He and Moses are identified as those who spoke to Pharaoh.

Pharaoh is called king of Egypt, and the LORD says that by a strong hand he will let Israel go and drive them out of his land. Moses is commanded to speak to him, and Moses doubts that Pharaoh will listen to him.

The children of Israel are promised redemption from Egyptian burdens, adoption as the LORD's people, and the land sworn to the patriarchs. They do not listen to Moses because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage. The chapter lists the family heads of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), Exodus, Chapter 6
s: The LORD says he established his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as aliens. He says he has remembered it on hearing Israel's groaning, and it grounds his promise to bring Israel into the land he swore to give them.

l: forced labor of Israelites, Exodus, Chapter 6
s: The Egyptians keep the children of Israel in bondage, and the LORD has heard their groaning. He promises to bring them out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, rid them of the bondage, and redeem them with an outstretched arm and great judgments. The cruel bondage, with anguish of spirit, keeps the people from listening to Moses.

The LORD tells Moses he has been made as God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet, and announces that he will harden Pharaoh's heart and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt by great judgments. Moses (eighty) and Aaron (eighty-three) go to Pharaoh, where Aaron's rod becomes a serpent and swallows the rods of the Egyptian magicians, who had done the same with their enchantments. Pharaoh's heart stays hardened, so the LORD sends Moses to meet him at the river's bank with a demand to let the people go. Aaron then stretches out the rod and the waters of Egypt turn to blood, killing the fish and making the river foul. The magicians duplicate this too, Pharaoh turns away unmoved, the Egyptians dig for drinking water, and seven days pass.

The LORD makes Moses as God to Pharaoh, announces he will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply signs, and commands the rod miracle and the turning of the river to blood. He states that the Egyptians will know he is the LORD when he stretches out his hand and brings the children of Israel out by great judgments. He strikes the river, and seven days are fulfilled afterward.

Moses is told he is made as God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet, and he obeys the LORD's commands. He is eighty years old when he speaks to Pharaoh and is sent to meet Pharaoh at the river's bank to demand that the people be let go.

Aaron, eighty-three years old, serves as Moses' prophet and speaker to Pharaoh. He casts down his rod, which becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians' rods, and later stretches out the rod over the waters of Egypt so they turn to blood.

Pharaoh asks for a miracle, calls his wise men and sorcerers when Aaron's rod becomes a serpent, and does not listen to Moses and Aaron. After the river turns to blood and his magicians copy it, he turns and goes into his house without taking it to heart.

Egypt is the land where the LORD will stretch out his hand and multiply his signs and wonders. Its waters, including rivers, streams, pools and ponds, turn to blood, and blood is throughout the whole land, even in vessels of wood and stone.
The Egyptians are to know the LORD when he brings Israel out from among them. When the river becomes blood and foul, they cannot drink from it and dig around the river for water.

The children of Israel are called the LORD's armies and his people, whom he will bring out of Egypt by great judgments. Moses and Aaron are to demand Pharaoh let them go to serve the LORD in the wilderness.

Pharaoh's wise men, sorcerers and magicians cast down their rods, which become serpents by their enchantments, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs. They also turn water to blood with their enchantments, which leaves Pharaoh's heart hardened.

Aaron's rod becomes a serpent when cast down before Pharaoh and swallows the magicians' rods. It is the rod Moses is told to take to the river, and Aaron lifts it to strike the waters, turning them to blood.

l: river (the Nile waters of Egypt), Exodus, Chapter 7
s: The river is where Pharaoh goes out to the water in the morning and where Moses is to meet him. Struck with the rod, its waters turn to blood, its fish die, and it becomes foul and undrinkable.

l: blood plague (water turned to blood), Exodus, Chapter 7
s: The LORD announces and then carries out the plague through Aaron's rod, turning the river and all waters of Egypt to blood. The fish die, the river stinks, the Egyptians cannot drink, and the magicians replicate it. Seven days pass after the LORD struck the river.

The LORD says beforehand that he will harden Pharaoh's heart, and Pharaoh's heart is hardened after the serpent sign and again after the blood plague. Each time he does not listen, as the LORD had spoken, and the LORD calls his heart stubborn.

The LORD sends Moses to demand that Pharaoh let his people go, and brings three plagues on Egypt when Pharaoh refuses. Frogs cover the land, and Pharaoh promises to release the people if they are removed, but he hardens his heart once the frogs die. Aaron strikes the dust with his rod and it becomes lice on people and animals; the magicians cannot imitate this and say it is God's finger, yet Pharaoh still refuses. The LORD then sends swarms of flies on Egypt while setting apart the land of Goshen, and Pharaoh offers a compromise, but after Moses prays and the flies are removed he again refuses to let the people go.
